sub: Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association
q: All of the following insurers are required by Michigan law to be members of the Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association EXCEPT:
choices: A surplus lines insurer writing coverage in Michigan
An authorized insurer writing workers' compensation insurance in Michigan
An authorized insurer writing homeowners insurance in Michigan
An authorized insurer writing private passenger automobile insurance in Michigan
explain: Membership is required of insurers authorized to write non-life/non-disability insurance in Michigan. An insurer used solely through the surplus lines chapter (chapter 19) is not an authorized insurer for this purpose, so it is not a member and its insureds are not protected.

sub: Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association
q: The Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association's per-claim cap does NOT apply to which of the following covered claims?
choices: A homeowners dwelling claim
A commercial property claim
A commercial general liability claim
A claim for no-fault PIP benefits
explain: MCL 500.7925(6) caps covered claims at $5,000,000 (CPI-adjusted; $7,980,000 for 2026), but the cap does not apply to worker's compensation claims or PIP benefits under section 3107.
source: MCL 500.7925(6); DIFS Bulletin 2026-04-INS

sub: Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association
q: Under Michigan law, a claim by or against an insured is not a covered claim of the Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association if the insured's net worth exceeds a statutory base amount, before the annual inflation adjustment, of:
explain: The statute sets the net worth limit at $25,000,000, adjusted each January 1 for CPI ($39,920,000 for 2026). $5,000,000 is the base per-claim cap, a different limit.
source: MCL 500.7925(4); DIFS Bulletin 2026-04-INS

sub: Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association
q: When the Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association pays unearned premium claims of an insolvent insurer, no refund is made for an amount less than:
explain: MCL 500.7925(2)(a) provides that a refund of less than $50 shall not be made. $500 is the statutory base maximum unearned premium per person (CPI-adjusted; $2,063 for 7/1/2026-6/30/2027).
source: MCL 500.7925(2)(a); DIFS Bulletin 2026-13-INS

sub: Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association
q: After a receiver is appointed for an insolvent insurer, the Michigan Property and Casualty Guaranty Association continues coverage under the insurer's in-force policies until they expire, are replaced, or are canceled by the association, but in no event for more than how long after the appointment?
choices: 10 days
30 days
60 days
6 months
explain: Coverage continues no more than 30 days after the receiver's appointment. The association may also cancel those policies on 10 days' written notice. The 6-month figure is the automatic stay of court proceedings.

q: Under Michigan's mandatory fire policy provisions, a fire policy must provide, at a minimum, coverage for:
choices: Replacement cost of the property, without deduction for depreciation
Market value of the property, excluding land
Agreed value of the property as stated in the declarations
Actual cash value of the property at the time of loss
explain: MCL 500.2833(1)(a) requires, at a minimum, coverage for the actual cash value of the property at the time of loss. Replacement cost may be provided, but it is not the statutory minimum.

q: Which of the following is NOT one of the provisions Michigan law requires in every fire insurance policy?
choices: Coverage is suspended while the dwelling is vacant for more than 30 days
There can be no abandonment of property to the insurer
The insurer may repair, rebuild, replace, or take the property
The policy takes effect at 12:01 a.m. standard time at the location of the property
explain: MCL 500.2833(1) requires the policy to state the conditions that suspend or restrict coverage, but it does not mandate a 30-day vacancy suspension. The 12:01 a.m. effective time, no abandonment, and the insurer's option to repair or take the property are all required provisions.

q: A Michigan insured submits proof of the amount of a fire loss to his insurer, and Michigan's 25% fire-loss withholding law does not apply. Under Michigan's mandatory fire policy provisions, the loss is payable within how many days after the insurer receives that proof?
choices: 10 days
30 days
60 days
90 days
explain: MCL 500.2833(1)(p) requires payment within 30 days after receipt of proof of the amount of loss, except as provided in 500.2845. The unendorsed ISO HO form's 60-day loss payment condition yields to the statute.
source: MCL 500.2833(1)(p); ISO HO 00 03 05 11 Sec. I Cond. J

q: Under Michigan's mandatory fire policy provisions, the insured must commence a lawsuit against the insurer:
choices: Within 1 year after the loss or any longer period in the policy, tolled from notice of loss until formal denial
Within 1 year after the loss, even if the policy states a longer period, with no tolling of the time limit
Within 2 years after the insurer receives the sworn proof of loss, tolled while any appraisal is pending
Within 3 years after the loss, tolled from notice of loss until formal denial
explain: MCL 500.2833(1)(q) requires suit within 1 year after the loss or the policy's period, whichever is longer. The time is tolled from when the insured notifies the insurer of the loss until the insurer formally denies liability.

q: A Michigan insured cancels her fire insurance policy midterm. Under Michigan's mandatory fire policy provisions, the insurer's minimum earned premium may not be less than:
choices: The short-rate premium for the expired time
10% of the annual premium
The pro rata premium for the expired time or $25, whichever is greater
The pro rata premium for the expired time or $50, whichever is greater
explain: MCL 500.2833(1)(h) allows the insured to cancel at any time, and the minimum earned premium is the greater of the pro rata premium for the expired time or $25. The same minimum applies when the insurer cancels under (1)(i).

q: An insured and insurer disagree on the amount of a fire loss, and the insured makes a written demand for appraisal under Michigan law. The two appraisers cannot agree on an umpire within 15 days. Who may select the umpire?
choices: The Director of the Department of Insurance and Financial Services, at either party's request
The insurer, subject to the insured's approval
A circuit court judge in the county where the loss occurred or the property is located
The American Arbitration Association, at the request of either party
explain: MCL 500.2833(1)(m): if the appraisers cannot agree on an umpire within 15 days, either party may ask a circuit court judge in the county where the loss occurred or the property is located to select one. A written agreement signed by any 2 of the 3 sets the loss.

q: Under Michigan's mandatory fire policy provisions, how are appraisal costs paid?
choices: The insurer pays all appraisal costs, including both appraisers and the umpire
The losing party pays all costs, as determined by the umpire
The insured pays all costs if the award is less than the insurer's last offer
Each party pays its own appraiser; the umpire and other costs are split equally
explain: Each appraiser is paid by the party that selected that appraiser. Other appraisal expenses and the umpire's compensation are paid equally by the insured and insurer. Each party must also select its appraiser within 20 days after the written demand.

q: An insurer issued a new homeowners policy to an eligible person 40 days ago and now wants to terminate it for a reason other than nonpayment. Under the Essential Insurance Act, the termination can be effective no sooner than how many days after the notice is mailed?
choices: 10 days
20 days
30 days
45 days
explain: Generally, termination of home or auto insurance requires at least 30 days' notice stating each specific reason. A notice mailed or delivered within the first 55 days after initial issuance may be effective not less than 20 days after mailing.

q: Under Michigan's mandatory casualty policy provisions, an insurer may cancel a casualty policy, other than workers' compensation or mortgage guaranty insurance, by mailing the insured written notice of not less than:
choices: 5 days
10 days
20 days
30 days
explain: Section 3020(1)(b) requires not less than 10 days' written notice of cancellation by the insurer. A malpractice policy may be nonrenewed only on not less than 60 days' notice.

q: Under the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, as reauthorized in 2019, which statement is correct?
choices: The insurer deductible is 20% of its direct earned premium for the prior calendar year
The federal share of compensation is 90% of insured losses above the insurer's deductible
The program trigger is $100 million in aggregate industry insured losses
The program is permanent and has no termination date
explain: The insurer deductible is 20% of prior-year direct earned premium. The federal share is 80% (not 90%) and the program trigger is $200 million for 2020 and later. The program terminates December 31, 2027 unless extended; extension bills were pending in October 2026.

q: Under the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act (TRIA), an act may be certified as an act of terrorism only if the aggregate property and casualty insurance losses resulting from it exceed:
choices: $1 million
$5 million
$100 million
$200 million
explain: TRIA §102(1)(B)(ii) bars certification if aggregate P&C losses do not exceed $5,000,000. $200 million is the separate program trigger for federal payments. (A pending 2026 House bill would raise the $5 million figure to $10 million beginning in 2029.)

q: Under the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act (TRIA), who certifies that an event is an "act of terrorism"?
choices: The Secretary of Homeland Security, in consultation with the FBI Director and the Secretary of Defense
The President, with the consent of Congress
The Treasury Secretary, in consultation with the Homeland Security Secretary and the Attorney General
The NAIC, in consultation with the insurance commissioners of the affected states
explain: Certification is by the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Secretary of Homeland Security and the Attorney General. The decision to certify or not certify is final and not subject to judicial review.

sub: Termination of Authority to Represent Insurer
q: A property and casualty insurer terminates an independent producer's agency contract, and their written agreement says nothing about the producer's authority after termination. Under Michigan law, the producer may:
choices: Bind new risks and renew existing policies without insurer approval for 30 days after notice of termination
Renew each existing policy one time without insurer approval, but not bind any new risks
Not service existing policies or otherwise act for the insurer after receiving notice of termination
Service existing policies, but not bind new risks, renew, or increase the insurer's obligation without approval
explain: If the agreement does not address the post-termination period, the producer may continue servicing existing policies. The producer may not bind new risks, renew a policy, or increase the insurer's obligation without the insurer's approval. The insurer may not cancel or nonrenew policies because of the producer's termination.

sub: Termination of Authority to Represent Insurer
q: Under Michigan law, an insurer writing home and auto insurance in Michigan may terminate an independent producer's authority to represent it for all of the following reasons EXCEPT:
choices: Loss experience related to the geographic location of the producer's business
Submission of fewer than 25 home and auto applications in the preceding 12 months
Malfeasance
Breach of fiduciary duty or trust
explain: MCL 500.1209(2) permits termination for malfeasance, breach of fiduciary duty or trust, violation of the Code, failure to perform the contract, or fewer than 25 applications in 12 months. Subsection (3) forbids termination based primarily on geographic location or location-related loss experience.

q: Under the Essential Insurance Act, which of the following persons is an "eligible person" for home insurance?
choices: An owner-occupant of a 3-family dwelling
A landlord who owns, but does not live in, a single-family rental house
A homeowner whose property taxes have been delinquent for 3 years
A homeowner convicted of arson 2 years ago
explain: An eligible person for home insurance is an owner-occupant or tenant of a house, condo or co-op unit, room, or apartment, or the owner-occupant of a dwelling of not more than 4 units. A non-occupying owner is not included. Also excluded: arson convictions within the preceding 5 years; property taxes delinquent 2 or more years.

q: Under the Essential Insurance Act, an insurer's underwriting rules for home insurance may be based on all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: A dwelling unoccupied more than 60 days with evidence of intent to vacate
The physical condition of the property, based on specific housing and safety code provisions
The age of the dwelling
Failure to correct, after written notice, a physical condition directly related to a paid claim
explain: Physical-condition rules must be objective, related to the insured perils, and based on specific code provisions 'without regard to the age of the structure.' Unoccupancy over 60 days with intent to vacate, and failure to correct a condition after notice, are permitted bases.

q: Under the Essential Insurance Act, when an applicant who applied orally for home insurance is declined, the insurer or agent must:
choices: Provide the specific reasons in writing by certified mail within 10 days
Provide reasons only if the applicant files a complaint with DIFS
Refer the applicant to the Michigan Basic Property Insurance Association, with no explanation required
State each specific reason and offer a written explanation if requested within 90 days
explain: Each specific reason for a declination must be given. If the request was in writing, the explanation must be in writing. If it was oral, an oral explanation may be given, and a written one must be offered if the applicant requests it within 90 days. Refusing to provide an application form counts as a declination.

q: Under the Essential Insurance Act, refusing to insure, refusing to continue to insure, or limiting coverage because of the location of the risk is called:
choices: Rebating
Churning
Twisting
Redlining
explain: MCL 500.2108(8) requires every filing to specify that the insurer will not refuse to insure, refuse to continue to insure, or limit coverage because of the location of the risk. The statute calls that practice redlining and prohibits it.

q: Under the 1988 ISO Dwelling Policy Basic Form (DP-1), which perils are covered when no premium is shown for Extended Coverage or Vandalism or Malicious Mischief?
choices: Fire, lightning, and internal explosion
Fire, lightning, windstorm, and hail
Fire, lightning, and vandalism
All risks of direct physical loss except those excluded
explain: DP-1 covers fire or lightning and internal explosion. Paying the Extended Coverage premium adds windstorm or hail, explosion, riot or civil commotion, aircraft, vehicles, smoke, and volcanic eruption. V&MM is a separate optional premium.
source: ISO DP 00 01 07 88, Perils Insured Against 1A-1B, 2-9

q: How are Coverages A, B and C insured under the Dwelling Policy Special Form (DP-3)?
choices: Coverages A, B and C on an open-perils basis
Coverages A and B on an open-perils basis; Coverage C on a named-perils basis
Coverage A on an open-perils basis; Coverages B and C on a basic named-perils basis
Coverages A, B and C on a named-perils basis, including theft
explain: DP-3 insures Coverages A and B against risk of direct physical loss unless excluded. Coverage C personal property is covered only for the listed broad named perils, which do not include theft.
source: ISO DP 00 03 12 02, Perils Insured Against A-B

q: A landlord insures a rental dwelling she does not occupy under the Dwelling Policy Special Form (DP-3). She wants theft coverage for her appliances and furnishings in the building. Under ISO dwelling program rules, which endorsement is appropriate?
choices: No endorsement is needed
Broad Theft Coverage, on and off premises
Limited Theft Coverage, on premises only
Personal Liability Supplement
explain: Broad Theft (DP 04 72) is for owner-occupied dwellings and tenant named insureds, and may include off-premises coverage. Non-owner-occupied risks use Limited Theft Coverage (DP 04 73), on-premises only. The DP-3's own Coverage C perils do not include theft.
source: ISO Dwelling Policy Program Manual Rule 510.A; ISO DP 00 03 12 02, Coverage C perils

q: Under ISO dwelling program rules for the Broad Theft Coverage endorsement, off-premises theft coverage:
choices: May be purchased without on-premises coverage, at any limit the insured selects
Is available only for non-owner-occupied dwellings rented to tenants
Is included at 10% of the Coverage C limit
Requires on-premises coverage, at a limit no greater than the on-premises limit
explain: Off-premises coverage is available only when on-premises coverage is purchased. Its limit may not be greater than the on-premises limit. The manual's minimum limit is $1,000 each.
source: ISO Dwelling Policy Program Manual Rule 510.A.1

q: An owner-occupant insured under the Dwelling Policy Special Form (DP-3) has a covered fire that forces her family to live in a hotel. Which coverage pays the necessary increase in living expenses?
choices: Coverage B – Other Structures
Coverage C – Personal Property
Coverage D – Fair Rental Value
Coverage E – Additional Living Expense
explain: In the dwelling forms, Coverage D is Fair Rental Value (for the part rented to others) and Coverage E is Additional Living Expense. The DP-3 also provides up to 20% of Coverage A as additional insurance for D and E combined.
source: ISO DP 00 03 12 02, Coverages D-E; Other Coverage 5

q: Of the 1988 ISO dwelling forms DP-1 and DP-2 and the 2002 ISO DP-3, which settles losses to the dwelling at actual cash value rather than replacement cost?
choices: Basic Form (DP-1)
Broad Form (DP-2)
Special Form (DP-3)
Both the Broad Form (DP-2) and the Special Form (DP-3)
explain: The 1988 DP-1 settles covered losses at actual cash value, but not more than the cost to repair or replace. The 1988 DP-2 and the 2002 DP-3 pay replacement cost on buildings if insurance is at least 80% of replacement cost.
source: ISO DP 00 01 07 88, Cond. 5; ISO DP 00 02 07 88 and DP 00 03 12 02, Loss Settlement

q: The Personal Liability Supplement added to a dwelling policy provides:
choices: Coverage D – Fair Rental Value and Coverage E – Additional Living Expense
Coverage E – Personal Liability and Coverage F – Medical Payments to Others
Coverage L – Personal Liability and Coverage M – Medical Payments to Others
Coverage L – Loss of Use and Coverage M – Mortgagee Interest
explain: The dwelling forms contain no liability coverage. The Personal Liability Supplement adds Coverage L – Personal Liability and Coverage M – Medical Payments to Others. Its terms mirror Homeowners Section II, for example medical expenses incurred within 3 years and $1,000 damage to property of others.
source: ISO DL 24 01 12 02, Coverages L-M

q: Under the Dwelling Under Construction endorsement, the Coverage A limit shown in the Declarations is:
choices: Fixed at the dwelling's full completed value from the first day of construction
Limited to the cost of materials delivered to the site, excluding the value of labor
Reduced by 50% until a certificate of occupancy is issued for the completed dwelling
Provisional, and scaled on any date by the ratio of actual to completed value
explain: DP 11 43 makes the Coverage A limit provisional. The actual amount of insurance on any date is that percentage of the provisional amount equal to the ratio of actual value to completed value. Premium is based on the average amount of insurance, and occupancy is permitted for 30 days after completion.

sub: Selected Endorsements - Automatic Increase in Insurance
q: The Automatic Increase in Insurance endorsement attached to a dwelling policy:
choices: Increases the Coverage C limit by 10% after each paid loss, up to the amount of the Coverage A limit
Restores the policy limits after a paid loss, without an additional premium
Increases Coverage A and B limits annually by the percentage shown, applied pro rata over the policy period
Increases all coverage limits to the dwelling's full replacement cost at each annual renewal
explain: DP 04 11 increases the declared Coverage A and B limits annually by the percentage shown in the policy, applied pro rata during the policy period.

q: Which homeowners form covers the dwelling, other structures and personal property on an open-perils basis?
choices: HO-2 Broad Form
HO-3 Special Form
HO-5 Comprehensive Form
HO-8 Modified Coverage Form
explain: HO-5 insures Coverages A, B, and C against risk of direct physical loss unless excluded. HO-3 is open perils on A and B but named perils on C. HO-2 and HO-8 are named perils.
source: ISO HO 00 05 10 00, Sec. I Perils; ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Perils

q: In the HO-6 (Unit-Owners Form), Coverage A – Dwelling covers:
choices: The entire condominium building, including the roof, the common areas and every other owner's unit
The roof, exterior walls and common areas of the building, but nothing inside the unit
The unit owner's furniture, clothing, electronics and other personal property kept inside the unit
Unit fixtures and improvements, and property the owner must insure under the association agreement
explain: HO-6 Coverage A covers alterations, appliances, fixtures, and improvements within the unit, real property pertaining exclusively to the unit, property that is the owner's responsibility under the association agreement, and structures solely owned at the location.
source: ISO HO 00 06 05 11, Sec. I Coverage A

q: Under the 2000 ISO HO-8 (Modified Coverage Form), theft coverage is:
choices: Excluded both on and off the residence premises
Limited to $1,000 per loss, on the residence premises only
Limited to 10% of Coverage C when off the residence premises
Unlimited, and covered both on and off the residence premises
explain: The 2000 HO-8 Theft peril excludes theft off the residence premises and limits recovery to $1,000 in any one loss caused by theft. Property in a bank, safe deposit company, or public warehouse is considered on the residence premises.
source: ISO HO 00 08 10 00, Sec. I Perils 9; PF&M ISO Homeowners Optional Endorsements (2014), HO 04 30

q: An insured with a 2000 ISO HO-8 (Modified Coverage Form) repairs the damaged home at the same site within 180 days. The insurer pays the lesser of the limit or the amount actually spent, but no more than:
choices: The cost of using common, functionally equivalent construction materials and methods
The original construction cost of the home, adjusted for inflation to the date of loss
The market value of the home, including the land, at the time of the loss
80% of the cost to replace the home with materials of like kind and quality
explain: The 2000 HO-8's building loss settlement is designed for homes whose replacement cost greatly exceeds market value. It pays repair costs with common, functionally equivalent materials and methods. If the insured does not repair, it pays the least of the limit, market value excluding land, or ACV.
source: ISO HO 00 08 10 00, Sec. I Cond. C.2

q: Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms, which of the following meets the HO-3 definition of "insured"?
choices: The named insured's 25-year-old son, a full-time graduate student who moved out of the family home to attend school
The named insured's 22-year-old daughter, a full-time college student who moved out of the family home to attend school
An unrelated 30-year-old roommate who lives in the home and shares the household expenses
The named insured's sister, who lives in her own home across town and visits on weekends
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, "insured" includes a full-time student who was a household resident before leaving for school, if under 24 and a relative, or under 21 and in an insured's care. The 25-year-old is too old. An unrelated adult roommate and a relative in her own household are not insureds.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Definitions B.5

q: Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms, a paid activity is not a "business" if no insured received more than what total compensation for it in the 12 months before the policy period?
explain: The 2011 "business" definition excludes activities for which no insured receives more than $2,000 in total compensation in the 12 months before the policy period. It also excludes volunteer work and certain home day care: mutual exchange, or care for a relative.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Definitions B.3

q: Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms, HO-3 Coverage B – Other Structures:
choices: Is limited to 10% of Coverage A, and using it does not reduce the Coverage A limit
Is limited to 10% of Coverage A, and using it reduces the Coverage A limit
Is limited to 20% of Coverage A, and using it does not reduce the Coverage A limit
Covers a detached garage the insured rents to a neighbor to store a business inventory
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, Coverage B is limited to 10% of the Coverage A limit, and its use does not reduce Coverage A. Coverage B excludes structures from which a business is conducted, and structures rented to non-tenants unless used solely as a private garage.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Coverage B

q: An HO-3 insured under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms has a $100,000 Coverage C limit. A covered fire destroys personal property usually kept at the insured's vacation cottage, which is not the residence premises. The most the policy will pay is:
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, property usually located at an insured's residence other than the residence premises is limited to 10% of Coverage C or $1,000, whichever is greater. 10% of $100,000 is $10,000. The same limit applies to property in a self-storage facility.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Coverage C.2

sub: Section I - Coverage C Special Limits
q: Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms, a burglar steals $4,000 of jewelry from the home of an insured with an HO-3 policy. Ignoring the deductible, the policy will pay:
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, jewelry, watches, furs, and precious and semiprecious stones have a $1,500 special limit for loss by theft. If the same jewelry were destroyed by fire, the special limit would not apply.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Coverage C.3.e

sub: Section I - Coverage C Special Limits
q: Which special limit of liability in the 2011 ISO Homeowners policy (HO-3) is stated correctly?
choices: Money, bank notes, and coins are limited to $500
Watercraft, including trailers and outboard motors, is limited to $2,500
Business property on the residence premises is limited to $1,500
Theft of firearms is limited to $2,500
explain: The HO-3 05 11 special limits are: money $200; theft of firearms $2,500; business property on premises $2,500 (off premises $1,500); watercraft $1,500.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Coverage C.3

q: Which of the following is NOT covered as personal property under Coverage C of the 2011 ISO Homeowners policy (HO-3)?
choices: The insured's pet dog
A riding lawn mower, not required to be registered, used solely to service the residence
A guest's luggage in the insured's home, at the insured's request
A model airplane not designed to carry people or cargo
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, Coverage C does not cover animals, birds, or fish. A non-registered motor vehicle used solely to service the residence, a guest's property in a residence occupied by an insured (at the insured's request), and model or hobby aircraft are covered.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Coverage C.1, C.4

q: A covered fire next door leads a civil authority to prohibit an insured from using his undamaged home. Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms, HO-3 Coverage D pays additional living expense and fair rental value for no more than:
choices: 72 hours
1 week
2 weeks
30 days
explain: In the 2011 HO-3, Civil Authority Prohibits Use covers ALE and fair rental value for no more than two weeks when a civil authority prohibits use because of direct damage to neighboring premises by a Peril Insured Against.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Coverage D.3

q: Which statement about the Trees, Shrubs and Other Plants additional coverage in the 2011 ISO Homeowners policy (HO-3) is correct?
choices: The limit is 5% of Coverage A, up to $500 for any one tree, shrub or plant
The limit is 10% of Coverage A, up to $1,000 for any one tree, shrub or plant
Windstorm is a covered peril for trees, shrubs and plants
Trees grown for business purposes are covered
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, trees, shrubs, plants, and lawns are covered up to 5% of the Coverage A limit, no more than $500 per tree. The covered perils are fire or lightning, explosion, riot, aircraft, non-resident vehicles, V&MM, and theft. Windstorm and property grown for business are not covered.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Add'l Cov. E.3

q: The Ordinance or Law additional coverage in the 2011 ISO Homeowners policy (HO-3) lets the insured use up to what amount for increased costs due to enforcement of building ordinances after a covered loss?
choices: 5% of Coverage A
10% of Coverage A
10% of Coverage C
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, the insured may use up to 10% of the Coverage A limit for increased costs from enforcing an ordinance or law, including related debris removal. This coverage is additional insurance. It does not cover loss in value or pollutant cleanup costs.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Add'l Cov. E.11

q: An HO-3 dwelling insured under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms has been vacant for 75 consecutive days when vandals break its windows and spray-paint the walls. The vandalism loss to the dwelling is:
choices: Not covered
Covered for the broken windows only
Covered at 50% of the loss
Covered in full
explain: The 2011 HO-3 Coverages A and B exclude vandalism and malicious mischief, and any ensuing loss from the wrongful act, if the dwelling has been vacant for more than 60 consecutive days immediately before the loss. A dwelling being constructed is not considered vacant.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Perils A.2.c(4)

q: All of the following are Section I exclusions in the Homeowners policy (HO-3) EXCEPT:
choices: Earthquake
Water that backs up through sewers or drains
Neglect of an insured to use all reasonable means to save property at and after a loss
Accidental discharge of water from within a plumbing system on the residence premises
explain: Sewer or drain backup (Water exclusion), earth movement, and neglect are Section I exclusions. Accidental discharge or overflow of water from a plumbing, heating, air conditioning, or sprinkler system or a household appliance is covered, including necessary tear-out.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Excl. A.2, A.3, A.5; Sec. I Perils A.2.c Exception

q: An HO-3 dwelling insured for $210,000 has a replacement cost of $300,000. A covered loss costs $40,000 to repair and has an actual cash value of $28,000. Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms and ignoring the deductible, what will the insurer pay after repairs are complete?
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, 80% of the $300,000 replacement cost is $240,000, so the home is underinsured. The insurer pays the greater of ACV ($28,000) or ($210,000 / $240,000) x $40,000 = $35,000. It therefore pays $35,000.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. D.2.b

q: Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms (HO-3), the insurer will pay replacement cost before repair or replacement is complete only if the cost to repair or replace is:
choices: Less than $1,000, with no percentage test
Less than 5% of the insurance on the building and less than $2,500
Less than 10% of the insurance on the building, with no dollar cap
Less than the deductible
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, the insurer pays no more than ACV until actual repair or replacement is complete. The exception is when the cost is both less than 5% of the insurance on the building and less than $2,500. The insured may claim ACV first and notify the insurer within 180 days of the intent to repair.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. D.2.d-e

q: In the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms (HO-3), the Duties After Loss condition says the insured must send the insurer a signed, sworn proof of loss within:
choices: 30 days after the date of the loss
60 days after the insurer's request
90 days after notice of the loss
1 year after the loss
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, the insured must send a signed, sworn proof of loss within 60 days after the insurer's request. Other duties include prompt notice, notifying police of theft, protecting the property, preparing an inventory, and submitting to examination under oath.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. C.8

q: Whose medical bills, incurred within 3 years of the accident, would Coverage F – Medical Payments to Others pay under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms (HO-3)?
choices: The named insured's spouse, who fell down the stairs at home
The named insured's 10-year-old son, who broke his arm at a playground
A guest who tripped on the insured's sidewalk while visiting
The named insured, who was injured mowing the lawn
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, Coverage F pays necessary medical expenses incurred or medically ascertained within three years of the accident. It does not apply to you or regular residents of your household, except residence employees. A guest injured on the insured location with permission is covered.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. II Coverage F

q: In the Homeowners policy (HO-3), the insurer's duty to settle or defend a claim under Coverage E – Personal Liability ends when:
choices: The suit is found by the court to be groundless, false, or fraudulent
The insured is found to be more than 50% at fault for the claimant's injury
The policy expires before the suit is filed
The limit for the occurrence is exhausted by payment of a judgment or settlement
explain: Coverage E provides a defense at the insurer's expense even if the suit is groundless, false, or fraudulent. The duty to settle or defend ends when the limit for the occurrence is exhausted by payment of a judgment or settlement.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. II Coverage E

q: An HO-3 named insured owns a motorboat with a 40-horsepower outboard motor that she bought two years before the current policy period and never declared or reported to the insurer. She negligently injures a swimmer while operating it. Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms, Coverage E – Personal Liability:
choices: Does not apply
Applies up to the Coverage E limit
Applies, but only if the boat is less than 26 feet long
Applies, but only up to $1,500
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, owned outboard motors over 25 total horsepower are covered only if acquired during the policy period, or if acquired before it and declared at inception or reported in writing within 45 days of acquisition. Neither applies here, so the Watercraft Liability exclusion applies. The Watercraft endorsement (HO 24 75) can add this coverage.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. II Excl. B.2.c(2); PF&M 2014 (HO 24 75)

q: Which loss would be covered by the Damage to Property of Others additional coverage in Section II of the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms (HO-3)?
choices: The insured's 15-year-old intentionally smashes a neighbor's mailbox
The insured's 8-year-old accidentally breaks a borrowed video game console
The insured damages his own car while backing out of the garage
The insured damages a customer's equipment while running his home business
explain: Under the 2011 HO-3, Damage to Property of Others pays up to $1,000 per occurrence at replacement cost. It does not cover damage caused intentionally by an insured 13 or older, property owned by an insured, business-related damage, or damage arising from motor vehicles.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. II Add'l Cov. C

q: In the Homeowners policy (HO-3), Coverage E – Personal Liability excludes property damage to property rented to, occupied or used by, or in the care of an insured, except damage caused by:
choices: Theft, vandalism, or windstorm
Water, collapse, or freezing
Fire, smoke, or explosion
Any accidental occurrence
explain: Property damage to property rented to or in the care of an insured is excluded under Coverage E, except damage caused by fire, smoke, or explosion. For example, a tenant who accidentally starts a fire in a rented home has liability coverage.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. II Excl. F.3

q: Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners program, an insured's Scheduled Personal Property endorsement covers $20,000 of scheduled jewelry. She buys a new $8,000 ring and loses it two weeks later. She reports the new ring and the loss to the insurer the next day. How much does the endorsement pay?
choices: Nothing
explain: Newly acquired jewelry, furs, cameras and musical instruments in a class that is already scheduled are covered for the lesser of 25% of that class's limit or $10,000, if reported within 30 days. 25% of $20,000 is $5,000. The endorsement (HO 04 61) is open-perils, so a mysterious disappearance is covered, and no deductible applies. The $1,500 figure is the homeowners Coverage C special limit for theft of jewelry, which does not control here.
source: PF&M Analysis: HO 04 61 Scheduled Personal Property Endorsement (July 2017); Texas HO 23 03 05 11

sub: Selected Endorsements - Personal Property Replacement Cost
q: Which item remains on an actual cash value basis under the 2011 ISO Personal Property Replacement Cost endorsement for homeowners policies?
choices: A rare antique clock that cannot be replaced
A ten-year-old refrigerator in daily use
A three-year-old living room sofa in good condition
Wall-to-wall carpeting in the bedrooms
explain: The 2011 edition of HO 04 90 settles Coverage C, carpeting, appliances, awnings, and outdoor equipment at replacement cost. These are ineligible and remain at ACV: antiques, fine arts, and rarities that cannot be replaced; memorabilia and collectors' items; items not in good or workable condition; obsolete stored items. If the cost exceeds $500, only ACV is paid until the item is replaced.
source: ISO HO 04 90 05 11, B. and C.2

q: Which statement is correct about the 2000 ISO Earthquake endorsement for homeowners policies?
choices: The deductible is a flat $500 per earthquake
Shocks within a 72-hour period are considered a single earthquake
Exterior masonry veneer is covered unless the insured chooses to exclude it
Flood or tidal wave caused by an earthquake is covered
explain: HO 04 54 treats shocks within 72 hours as one earthquake. The deductible is a percentage of the greater of the Coverage A or C limit (minimum $250 in the 10 00 edition). Exterior masonry veneer is excluded unless that exclusion is removed, and flood caused by earthquake is excluded.

q: An insured operates a piano-teaching studio in her home and adds the 2000 ISO Permitted Incidental Occupancies – Residence Premises endorsement to her homeowners policy. Which statement is correct?
choices: The $2,500 business property special limit still applies to her studio equipment
The endorsement converts the homeowners policy into a businessowners policy for the studio
Section II covers liability arising from the studio, except bodily injury to its employees
An other structure from which the studio is run is covered under Coverage B
explain: HO 04 42 (10 00 edition) removes the Section II business exclusion for the described business and applies the full Coverage C limit to that business's property. It still excludes BI to employees of the business. A described other structure is insured for its own scheduled limit instead of under Coverage B.

q: Which one of the following would be covered by adding the Personal Injury endorsement to a homeowners policy?
choices: The insured's child damages a neighbor's fence
The insured's dog bites a mail carrier
A guest slips on the insured's icy steps
A neighbor sues the insured for slander
explain: HO 24 82 adds personal injury coverage: false arrest, detention or imprisonment, malicious prosecution; libel, slander, or defamation; invasion of privacy; and wrongful eviction or entry. Dog bites, slip-and-falls, and property damage are bodily injury or property damage already covered under Coverage E.
source: PF&M Analysis: ISO Homeowners Optional Coverage Endorsements (July 2014), HO 24 82

q: The Business Pursuits endorsement to a homeowners policy is designed to cover the liability of an insured who:
choices: Works as a schoolteacher or salesperson for an employer
Is a partner in a law firm with several other partners
Is the sole owner and operator of a retail store
Runs a licensed day care center from home
explain: HO 24 71 covers liability arising from an insured's business activities when the insured is not the sole owner or a partner. Examples are clerical employees, salespersons, collectors, messengers, and teachers; teachers may add corporal punishment coverage.
source: PF&M Analysis: ISO Homeowners Optional Coverage Endorsements (July 2014), HO 24 71

q: A homeowner runs a day care in her home, caring for three unrelated neighborhood children for pay and earning about $15,000 a year. Under the 2011 ISO Homeowners forms, liability arising from the day care under an unendorsed HO-3 policy is:
choices: Covered in full under Coverage E – Personal Liability
Excluded as a business activity
Covered up to $2,000 of annual receipts
Covered only under Coverage F – Medical Payments to Others
explain: Day care run for pay is a "business" under HO 00 03 05 11: it is an occupation, and it is an activity engaged in for compensation. The definition's home day care carve-outs cover only care paid for by a mutual exchange of services or care for a relative, and the $2,000 exception could not apply because she earns far more than $2,000. Section II excludes business liability. The Home Day Care Coverage endorsement (HO 04 97) can add coverage.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Definitions B.3, Sec. II Excl. E.2; PF&M 2014 (HO 04 97)

sub: Selected Endorsements - Limited Fungi, Wet or Dry Rot, or Bacteria
q: Under the 2002 ISO Limited Fungi, Wet or Dry Rot, or Bacteria Coverage endorsement for the HO-3 and HO-5, which limits are pre-printed in the schedule?
choices: Section I: $5,000; Coverage E aggregate: $25,000
Section I: $10,000; Coverage E aggregate: $50,000
Section I: $25,000; Coverage E aggregate: $100,000
Section I: no limit; Section II: $10,000 per occurrence
explain: The HO 04 27 schedule shows $10,000 for the Section I additional coverage, which caps the total of all fungi, wet or dry rot, or bacteria loss plus the costs of removal, tear-out and testing, and a $50,000 Section II Coverage E aggregate sublimit. That sublimit is within, not in addition to, the Coverage E limit. Companies may file different amounts.
source: ISO HO 04 27 04 02, Schedule

sub: Selected Endorsements - Home Business Insurance Coverage
q: Which ISO endorsement is a self-contained, extensive form providing both property and liability coverage for a described business operated in the insured's residence or an other structure on the residence premises?
choices: Business Pursuits
Scheduled Personal Property
Personal Injury
Home Business Insurance Coverage
explain: HO 07 01 Home Business Insurance Coverage is structured like a self-contained policy, giving property and liability coverage for a described business run from the residence or a structure on the residence premises. Business Pursuits covers liability for business activities of an insured who is not an owner or partner.
source: PF&M Analysis: ISO Homeowners Optional Coverage Endorsements (July 2014), HO 07 01

sub: Section II - Coverage E and F
q: In the ISO Homeowners program manual, the minimum limits of liability for Section II are:
choices: Coverage E $25,000; Coverage F $1,000 per person
Coverage E $50,000; Coverage F $500 per person
Coverage E $100,000; Coverage F $1,000 per person
Coverage E $300,000; Coverage F $5,000 per person
explain: The ISO Homeowners manual's minimum limits are $100,000 for Coverage E – Personal Liability and $1,000 for Coverage F – Medical Payments to Others, for all forms. Higher limits are available for additional premium.
source: ISO Homeowners Policy Program Manual Table 301 as reproduced in RIJRA HO Manual (eff. 11/1/2021)

q: Under the Concealment or Fraud condition of the Homeowners policy (HO-3), if one insured intentionally conceals a material fact relating to the insurance, Section I property coverage is:
choices: Denied only to the insured who committed the fraud
Provided to no insureds under the policy
Reduced by 50%
Unaffected unless the fraud occurred before the loss
explain: Section I Condition R states that coverage is provided to no insureds if, before or after a loss, an insured intentionally concealed or misrepresented a material fact, engaged in fraudulent conduct, or made false statements. Under Section II (Cond. J), coverage is denied only to the insured involved.
source: ISO HO 00 03 05 11, Sec. I Cond. R; Sec. II Cond. J
